title: Opportunities and Challenges in Legal AI
author: Aksh Garg · Megan Ma

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source supports broad claims that legal AI may reduce costs and improve workflow efficiency, but it does not address the cluster’s central access-to-justice proposition: direct-to-consumer use shifts reliability and verification risks onto poorly equipped users. Its focus on startup adoption barriers and market opportunities provides insufficient evidence to establish support or opposition.
qs: As the complexity of cases grows and client expectations rise, AI offers an unprecedented opportunity to reshape legal workflows by improving efficiency and reducing costs in most areas of the legal stack.
At a high-level, we clustered these challenges to the difficulty of obtaining quality data, the law firm business model, the scattered subvertical, platform constraints, and cultural resistance.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production

kp.k: Lower model costs expand legal automation opportunities
kp.d: The authors identify text-intensive, repetitive legal work—basic research, document review and case preparation—as an opportunity for generative AI. They cite a $1 Trillion global legal market and Ma et al.'s reported funding of ~700M between Jan 2023 - Feb 2024. They describe per-token LLM costs as falling roughly 10x annually and GPT, Claude and Gemini context windows reaching 128K, 200K and 1M tokens respectively. These developments are presented as enabling cheaper processing of lengthy legal documents, rather than as measured evidence of realised savings across firms.
qs: lawyers spend a disproportionate amount of time on repetitive tasks such as basic research, document review, and case preparation.
funding for LegalTech startups totaled ~700M between Jan 2023 - Feb 2024.

These changes are enabling lawyers to process hundred-page briefs, the typical length of legal documents, at a fraction of the costs of actual lawyers doing the work, resulting in new levels of savings.

kp.k: Proprietary data restricts legal AI development
kp.d: The authors argue that sensitive, guarded legal data creates a circular barrier: effective systems need proprietary information, but firms want demonstrated benefits before sharing it. They regard public patent and court datasets, including Free Law Project materials, as starting points rather than sufficient foundations for competitive tools. Published final work products also omit intermediate reasoning stages. These claims derive from the authors' research-prototyping experience, not a reported comparative study.
qs: While publicly available datasets, such as patent data and/or other court data made available via Free Law Project, provide a starting point, proprietary data is essential for building tools with real competitive value.

Moreover, the data that is released and published often only contains the final product, missing the intermediary stages in the pipeline, which are crucial for building reasoning capabilities within these models.

kp.k: Confidentiality makes parsing and interface expertise essential
kp.d: The authors recommend structured pilots and design partnerships to gain data access, while describing practical limitations from CodeX's automated redlining training work. Confidentiality requires redacted PDFs, which then need complex parsing and translation into insights usable in MS Word. They argue that these obstacles can favour teams with parsing and UI/UX expertise over founders whose backgrounds are predominantly machine learning.
qs: The best way founders can attempt to break this data wall is via well-structured pilots and design partners.
However, to protect client confidentiality, all shared data must necessarily be passed through redaction software, which generates PDFs with blacked out regions.
This often means that the best teams suited for these tasks have strong parsing and UI/UX backgrounds, rather than AI ones.

kp.k: Historical firm structures intertwine production, apprenticeship and reputation
kp.d: The authors trace organisational inertia to the Cravath System's profit-oriented pyramid of partners and associates, internal promotion, and insular apprenticeship. They argue that corporate relationships deepening in the 1960s reinforced trust, reputation and individual practitioners as organising principles. These structures persisted despite in-house departments and alternative legal service providers. This is a historical explanation for resistance to organisational and technological change, not an empirical finding that AI has already altered staffing ratios.
qs: There were fundamentally only two “classes” of professionals: partners and associates.
Furthermore, as partners are largely chosen within the firm, apprenticeship and culture hail from a rather insular heritage.
In effect, work product creation in the profession and skill development and training are intimately interrelated.
Even amidst changes, including the rise of in-house legal departments and alternative legal service providers, the law firm remained focused on the individual practitioner and their proteges.

kp.k: Hourly billing weakens incentives for AI efficiency
kp.d: The authors argue that reputation and information asymmetry displaced explicit measures of legal work quality, leaving time as a proxy for value. Hourly revenue therefore discourages efficiency-enhancing AI, while corporate acceptance of hourly billing reduces urgency to innovate. Fixed-fee transitions are described as gradual and difficult. They nevertheless report observations at Ashurst, Baker McKenzie and Wilson Sonsini that applying AI to inefficient junior-associate tasks can produce more significant benefits for clients.
qs: Therefore, time and billing on time spent became a proxy for value, as value generated from the work could not be measured concretely.
This creates a structural disincentive for law firms to adopt efficiency-enhancing technologies like AI, as reducing hours worked translates to reduced revenue.
While some firms are exploring alternatives, such as fixed-fee pricing, the transition is gradual and fraught with challenges.

We have observed from certain future-forward firms Ashurst, Baker McKenzie, and Wilson Sonsini that these areas of higher inefficiency have made the relative lift gained from using AI more significant to clients.

kp.k: Microsoft dependence constrains legal AI interfaces
kp.d: Drawing on their redlining work, the authors describe high migration friction away from Microsoft Office and consequent dependence on its interface limitations. They report difficulty displaying programmatic line- or word-level edits, sometimes requiring whole-paragraph replacement. They propose a lawyer-facing copilot with autocomplete and section insertion as an ideal interface, but identify short-term obstacles to implementing event-triggered functionality in Word.
qs: Lawyers are deeply integrated into the Microsoft Office suite, and getting lawyers to AI-first platforms presents high migration friction (i.e. complex change management).

In our personal redlining work, for example, we found that line/word level edits made programmatically are really difficult to show on the UI - instead you have to replace an old paragraph with a new paragraph, making changes hard to process and identify.
Furthermore, an ideal interface might resemble a legal copilot, with text autocomplete, and section insertion enabled.

kp.k: Targeted AI editing trades off global reasoning
kp.d: The authors argue that LLMs struggle with the surgical edits lawyers make and that regenerating 100+ page documents creates hallucination risks. Their research explored an agentic workaround that identifies relevant sections before generating only the content to insert, remove or edit. They report improved results but reduced global reasoning accuracy, without quantitative performance measures, and recommend further research on pointwise editing.
qs: Additionally, LLMs are bad pointwise editors.
Our work explored workarounds to this using an agentic approach, where we first identify relevant sections and only have the LLM generate new content for the section to be inserted/removed/edited.
This tends to improve results; however, it reduces global reasoning accuracy.

kp.d: The authors use illustrative calculations, not observed contract data: 100 seats per firm at $100/month would yield around $120K annually, while 1000 seats would yield $1.2M/yr. They argue that these revenues can struggle to justify upfront sales costs. Large firms' specialised demands require bespoke products and multiple product lines, pushing startups toward consultancy-like delivery, while privacy and proprietary-data dependence limit network effects.
qs: Even generously assuming 100 seats added per firm and $100/month seats, yearly revenue per contract would only be around $120K.
Even expanding to 1000 seats would restrict revenue to $1.2M/yr, making the upfront sales costs hard to justify.
These firm-to-firm differences, in turn, slow fast distribution as multiple product lines need to be maintained – positioning a tech startup as pseudo consultancy.
Furthermore, data privacy issues mean that it is very difficult to have true network effects.

kp.k: Long sales cycles favour trust and distribution expertise
kp.d: From their own law-firm pilots, the authors report sales cycles of 3 - 18 months because partners, IT teams and innovation leaders must agree. They characterise most contemporary AI tools as optional rather than essential, requiring repeated selling and separate pilots. They recommend strong go-to-market connections and experience, supplemented where necessary by legal cofounders, advisers or early hires who can accelerate trust-building.
qs: Through experience from our own pilots with our partnered law firms, we discovered that adoption requires buy-in from multiple stakeholders—partners, IT teams, and innovation leaders—which, for startups, often translates to long sales cycle (3 - 18 months).
In many ways, this makes an ideal legal AI founder one who has strong go-to- market connections and experience rather than a purely technical background.
There are certainly ways to bridge these deficits – for example, bringing on legal cofounders, advisors, or early hires, who can expedite the trust-building phase.

kp.k: Pilot participation can misrepresent commercial traction
kp.d: Conversations with partners at prominent BigLaw firms lead the authors to warn that firms test many external products simultaneously and pilot-to-paying-customer conversion can be low. Trials typically involve groups of 20-50 people rather than firm-wide adoption. No conversion percentage or interview sample size is reported. The recommendation is to demonstrate clear ROI on a specific, high-pain workflow rather than treat design partnerships as evidence of scalable revenue.
qs: First, the conversion rates between acquiring pilots to acquiring paying customers can be surprisingly low.

Additionally, these pilots often involve a specific group within the firm (typically on the order of 20-50 people) testing out your product and sharing feedback on it and other products at the end of the trial period.
To make a lasting impression, founders should focus on a specific problematic workflow to improve, as such a lift on a high-pain workflow can leave a lasting impression.

kp.k: Partner personas could scale expertise and junior training
kp.d: The authors propose small, personalised LLMs trained on curated partner knowledge as an alternative to a general-purpose AI lawyer. The rationale is that legal business depends on individual relationships, styles and experience. Suggested applications include simulating stakeholder responses to policy or firm-structure changes and explaining partners' redlines to junior attorneys using historical examples. These are prospective uses associated with forthcoming research, not established training or simulation outcomes.
qs: These personas hinge on the core thesis that we don't want to make a general all-purpose AI lawyer, but one that is specifically geared towards a partner’s background and experiences.
For example, consider running simulations of personas of different stakeholders responding to changes in policies or firm structure.
Alternatively, these personas can be used to educate junior attorneys faster by injecting additional context into redlines from their partners using partner personas.

kp.k: Computational law promises earlier checks but faces ambiguity
kp.d: The authors recommend experimenting with composable, formally verifiable building blocks for legal documents, hypothesising that formal representations of legal strategies could reduce hallucination. They criticise approaches that apply a checking model only after drafting because divergence may arise earlier. Their proposed formal verifiability is a technical mechanism, not evidence that human checking can be eliminated; they explicitly recognise that natural language and legal subjectivity make guarantees difficult.
qs: The underlying thesis here is that it is possible to express legal strategies in a formally verifiable language to reduce the risk of hallucination.
Unfortunately, most verification methods right now involve generating drafts and then applying a verifiability model at the end.
Additionally, many areas of law are subjective, where it is difficult to arrive at these explicitly correct answers.

kp.k: Patent retrieval offers comparatively aligned adoption incentives
kp.d: The authors identify structured, public patent data as lowering entry barriers and predict that semantic, graph-based and agentic retrieval will disrupt prior art searches, invalidity analyses and patentability assessments. Their proposed mechanism is faster, cheaper retrieval that frees attorneys for drafting and substantive arguments. Because many large firms already outsource prior art searching, they argue that adopting these products need not directly reduce law-firm billable hours.
qs: Another promising area for AI is within patent law, where the data is typically well-structured and publicly available.

We anticipate AI tools like semantic retrieval, graph-based retrieval, and agentic retrieval will disrupt traditional workflows like prior art searches, invalidity analyses, and patentability assessments.

Additionally, given that many large firms explicitly ask external search firms to find prior art on their behalf, selling these products doesn’t result in explicit reduction in billable hours for law firms, increasing their openness to adopting them.

kp.k: Patent competition and retrieval limitations constrain differentiation
kp.d: The authors qualify the patent opportunity with increasing market saturation and commoditisation risk unless startups establish data or distribution advantages. They argue that embeddings can miss small-feature similarities relevant to infringement and that default embeddings poorly match patent language, requiring substantial upfront training investment. Recommended differentiation includes claim-dependency visualisations, patent-office database integration and assistance constructing arguments around prior art matches.
qs: The market for patent-related tools is becoming increasingly saturated, making differentiation difficult.

Furthermore, while embeddings-based searches are optimized for detecting macro level similarities, they tend to perform poorly when two patents are only weakly related on the basis of a small feature.
This means startups have to make significant upfront investments in training their embedding modules.

To stand out, AI solutions must not only improve efficiency but also offer clean visualizations of claim dependencies, seamless integration with patent office databases, and help attorneys craft arguments around prior art matches.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Garg and Ma argue that generative AI can substantially accelerate legal work, but that commercial adoption is constrained by data access, billing incentives, technical integration and fragmented demand. They identify legal personas, computational law and patent automation as promising directions rather than established transformations.
pts.d:
1. Efficiency and cost: The authors claim that LLMs can accelerate understanding and processing of large legal documents and repetitive research, review and case preparation. Falling inference costs and larger context windows make processing long briefs cheaper than having lawyers perform the work.
2. Data and product development: They argue that proprietary legal data is essential for competitive tools, but confidentiality and firms' reluctance to share it impede development. Published final documents omit intermediate work needed to build reasoning capabilities. Redaction, parsing and movement between PDFs and Word make parsing and interface skills particularly important for founders.
3. Business-model incentives: They argue that hourly billing discourages efficiency-enhancing AI because fewer hours mean less revenue, while clients' acceptance of hourly billing reduces pressure to innovate. They nevertheless report that AI applied to inefficient junior-associate tasks has produced more significant benefits for clients at certain forward-looking firms. They do not predict a quantified reduction in associate employment or a specific replacement staffing structure.
4. Technical limitations: They claim that dependence on Microsoft Office limits AI-first interfaces, and that LLMs' tendency to regenerate entire documents rather than make surgical edits creates hallucination risks in long documents. Their section-targeted agentic approach improves results but reduces global reasoning accuracy.
5. Commercial scaling: They argue that narrow workflows, modest seat-based contract values, bespoke large-firm requirements and proprietary-data restrictions make startup sales and scaling difficult. Multi-stakeholder approval creates long sales cycles, while pilots can misleadingly suggest traction because conversion to paying customers may be low. Strong legal relationships and go-to-market capabilities can therefore matter more than a purely technical founding background.
6. Legal personas: They propose partner-specific models that preserve and scale individual expertise and client services. Possible uses include simulations of stakeholder responses to organizational changes and faster junior-attorney education through explanations of partners' redlines based on historical examples.
7. Computational law: They propose composable, formally verifiable representations of legal strategies to reduce hallucinations and detect divergence earlier than end-stage checking. They explicitly acknowledge the difficulty of verifying language and subjective legal questions.
8. Patent automation: They predict that semantic, graph-based and agentic retrieval will disrupt prior-art searches, invalidity analyses and patentability assessments. Faster, cheaper searches could shift attorneys' attention from document sifting to drafting and argument development. Where firms already outsource searches, these tools need not directly reduce firms' billable hours, improving adoption incentives. However, saturation, weak-feature retrieval failures and patent-language mismatch create differentiation and development challenges.
9. Broader outcome: Their conclusion conditionally anticipates faster, more efficient and more accessible legal services if these obstacles are navigated. It does not provide a concrete access-to-justice mechanism or a measured reduction in unmet civil legal need.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines the authors' CodeX prototyping and pilot experience, conversations with law-firm partners, illustrative commercial arithmetic and cited market/technology trends. The proposed future applications are not accompanied by quantified outcome evaluations.
pts.d:
1. Efficiency and cost: Garg and Ma cite approximately $700 million in LegalTech funding from January 2023 to February 2024, attributing that figure to The Generative AI Legal Landscape 2024 by Ma et al. They cite an Andreessen Horowitz figure by Guido Appenzeller for falling inference costs, describe an approximately tenfold annual reduction in per-token cost, and list GPT, Claude and Gemini context windows of 128K, 200K and 1M tokens respectively. These are offered as enabling trends and evidence of commercial interest, not as direct measurements of legal-task productivity. They also supply market and workload figures, including a $1 trillion global legal market, 65 million cases annually, 1.6 million patent filings and 450,000 U.S. law firms, without an accompanying source citation in the supplied text.
2. Data and technical constraints: Their principal evidence is hands-on CodeX work with law-firm partners, including an automated redlining training platform. They describe confidentiality-driven redaction, PDF parsing, Word integration problems and experiments with section-targeted generation. No benchmark scores or measured hallucination rates are reported for these experiments.
3. Billing incentives: Their explanation rests on a historical and organizational account of the Cravath system, reputation, information asymmetry and time-based pricing. They additionally report observations involving Ashurst, Baker McKenzie and Wilson Sonsini, but provide no quantified productivity or client-savings results for those firms.
4. Commercial adoption: The authors offer illustrative calculations: 100 seats at $100 per month yield $120,000 in annual revenue; 1,000 seats yield $1.2 million. These are assumptions used to illustrate sales economics, not observed contract averages. Their 3–18-month sales-cycle range comes from their own pilots. Conversations with prominent BigLaw partners support their account of simultaneous vendor trials, typically involving 20–50 users, and potentially low pilot conversion; no numerical conversion rate or sample size is supplied.
5. Future directions: Legal personas and computational law are presented primarily through theses, proposed use cases and a reference to forthcoming persona research, including multi-agent simulations. Patent automation claims are supported by reasoning about public structured data, existing search workflows and outsourced search procurement, alongside qualitative descriptions of embedding limitations. The paper supplies no comparative retrieval benchmark or deployment outcome for these proposals.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The adoption diagnosis describes conditions around January 2025; the innovation predictions have no fixed delivery dates and depend on overcoming specified data, workflow, incentive and reliability barriers.
pts.d:
1. Current enabling trends: The authors describe cost and context-window improvements as already enabling cheaper document processing at publication. The cited investment period is January 2023–February 2024. Their approximately tenfold annual inference-cost decline describes a trend, not an explicit guarantee that the same rate will continue.
2. Data access: Competitive development is conditional on obtaining usable proprietary information, potentially through well-structured pilots and design partners. Even willing partners cannot remove confidentiality, redaction and format-conversion constraints. Public structured patent data offers a relative exception to this barrier.
3. Billing and adoption: The revenue disincentive applies particularly where firms continue to bill by time. Fixed-fee adoption is described as gradual. Client pressure, demonstrable gains on inefficient tasks and founders' distribution advantages may create openings despite those incentives. The paper characterizes many AI products as currently optional rather than essential.
4. Interfaces and editing: Some copilot-like Word capabilities are characterized as blocked in the short term. Section-targeted generation is a current experimental workaround with a global-reasoning trade-off; improved pointwise editing remains a research opportunity.
5. Commercialization: The stated 3–18 months concerns sales cycles, not a forecast for industry-wide transformation. Successful commercialization is conditional on solving a high-priority workflow, demonstrating clear return on investment, building trust and securing adoption beyond pilots. Bespoke requirements and data privacy qualify expectations of easy scaling or network effects.
6. Legal personas: Benefits depend on highly curated, partner-specific training information and capturing individual experience and style. Simulations and accelerated training are prospective applications; the authors give no implementation deadline.
7. Computational law: Hallucination reduction is conditional on being able to represent legal strategies in formally verifiable form. The authors caution that correctness guarantees available in mathematics are difficult to replicate for language, especially subjective law. Their use of verification here concerns computational correctness mechanisms, not measured reductions in human checking work.
8. Patents: Disruption is predicted without a date. Adoption is more attractive where search is already outsourced and software does not directly displace billable firm work. Differentiation depends on data or distribution advantages, domain-adapted embeddings, useful visualizations, patent-office integration and support for building arguments. Saturation and weak-feature retrieval failures qualify the opportunity.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are legal-AI founders and vendors, law firms and their partners, junior attorneys, corporate clients and patent practitioners. Effects differ by firm size, billing arrangement and workflow.
pts.d:
1. Founders and legal-tech vendors: They face restricted data access, integration burdens, potentially small workflow-specific contracts, long sales cycles and uncertain pilot conversion. The authors suggest that parsing, interface design, legal relationships and distribution capabilities can be more commercially important than machine-learning expertise alone. Incumbent legal-tech vendors are described as treating proprietary data as a key source of value; they are not identified as alternative legal service providers.
2. Large versus small law firms: Large firms' specialized, high-value work drives bespoke products that are harder to scale across customers. Smaller firms are characterized as handling broader work with tighter resources. Hourly-billing firms face a tension between increased efficiency and revenue, whereas fixed-fee arrangements or already-outsourced workflows can change that incentive.
3. Partners, IT and innovation leaders: These stakeholders collectively influence purchasing and implementation. Partner expertise and client relationships are potential assets for persona-based systems, which could extend access to individual knowledge rather than create a single general-purpose AI lawyer.
4. Junior associates: Repetitive tasks are proposed as promising targets for efficiency gains. Persona-enriched explanations of redlines could accelerate learning. The paper notes the close relationship between producing work and professional training but does not quantify job displacement or predict the end of apprenticeship.
5. Corporate clients: Clients may receive efficiency and cost benefits, while large corporations' acceptance of hourly billing is described as reducing pressure for change. Some small and medium-sized businesses and more agile clients are described as pushing back against billing inefficiencies.
6. Patent attorneys, search providers and patent-tool startups: Attorneys could spend less time searching and more time drafting patents or developing invalidation arguments. Existing external search procurement creates an adoption opening, though the authors do not quantify its employment consequences for search firms. Startups benefit from accessible data but face saturation and technical investment requirements.
7. Public and service users: Greater accessibility is stated as a possible ultimate benefit. The paper does not separately examine underserved individuals, particular justice-gap populations or measured access-to-justice outcomes.
